--- title: "Calibration curves per chemical (4.5)" --- ::: {.cell} ::: For every targeted compound (`Quant` in the MS-DIAL comment), QuaNTA fits a calibration curve to the calibration samples (`Cal…` classes) and uses it to turn the signal of every sample into a concentration. Figure **4.5** of the app shows the curve of the compound selected in table **4.1**. Below is the same figure as in the app, with the example data (batch 1, Multivariate (PCA) normalization); here, choose the compound in the list or search it by name. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The figure has two modes; switch with the buttons, or with the arrow keys ← and →. The arrow keys ↑ and ↓ go to the previous and next compound (in the app, the rows of table 4.1). - **Calibration inspection** (first): every calibration point, each injection of a calibration sample, at its spiked (nominal) concentration and its measured signal. Points of the same concentration are replicates; with several batches, the symbol tells the batch. The colours tell the role of each level: - *Cal0* (red): the zero calibrant. Its signal gives the thresholds of the LOD (3×) and the LLOQ (10×, or the mean plus 3 / 10 standard deviations). On log axes, a concentration of 0 has no place: Cal0 is a short line at the left edge, at its signal. - *LOD* (blue): the lowest level whose mean signal is above the LOD threshold. - *Within limits* (green): the levels the curve is fitted on, from the LLOQ upwards. - *Above the ULOQ* (olive): levels in the curve but above its linear range. - *Out-of-range* (grey): levels not used for the curve. - **Final calibration model**: the fitted curve, the calibration points it was fitted on (black), and the QCs (blue; the QC group in the hover text) and study samples (by class) at the concentration the curve gives them. Values replaced by the LOD/LLOQ rules are open circles; their hover text tells the rule and the calculated concentration. In both modes: - **Shading**: dark grey below the LOD, light grey below the LLOQ, and olive above the ULOQ (dashed line), the top of the linear range. **Labels** at the top name each limit in its colour: *LOD* (blue) and *LLOQ* (purple), with a dotted line, or *LOD = LLOQ* (orange) when they are the same level, and *ULOQ* (olive). The ULOQ is always the actual top of the linear range, looked for among all calibration levels whatever the options (also above a curve shortened by *Optimize*): levels of the curve above it are in the olive area (unless *Enforce ULOQ* cut them off). - **Above the plot**, the parameters of the curve (model, R², LOD, LLOQ, ULOQ, highest calibration concentration, the curve used) and notes, e.g. why a curve is not valid. - **The title** names the compound, followed by the state of its curve in the colour of its row in table 4.1: *(not valid)* in red, *(global curve used)* in blue, *(removed before calibration)* in grey; nothing for a valid curve. - **Curve** (with several batches): the global curve, fitted on the calibration points of all batches, then the curve of every batch; the chosen batch's curve is shown first. The global curve is there for every compound, also when it is not used or not valid (its note says why). The key **G** goes to the next curve (in the report, after a click in the figure). In the app, the key **B** goes to the next batch (and *Global*), which shows that batch's curve first. **How to read it** - **Replicates should lie close together.** A level with widely spread replicates is a sign of a pipetting or injection problem; with the RSD% option, the LLOQ level must have an RSD% of at most 20%. - **Samples in the white area** are within the calibration range and quantified. - **Samples in the grey areas** are below the LLOQ (light) or the LOD (dark). Depending on the setting *Replace values below the LOD/LLOQ*, their concentrations are replaced (LLOQ/2 or LLOQ/4, open circles) or reported as *n.q.* / *n.d.*. - **Samples in the olive area** are above the ULOQ: within the curve but above its linear range, or extrapolated above its highest level. Treat these values with care, or dilute and re-measure. - **Samples in beige-grey** (quadratic curves only) are *capped*: a quadratic curve that bends down has a peak, and every signal at or above it gets the concentration of the peak. The real concentration is higher; dilute and re-measure. The exported tables give the peak as "Capped upper conc" in the Slope column. - **A curve far from its calibration points**, or points bending away at the top, suggests that the linear range is shorter than the calibration range; see the notes in table 4.1 and the option *Enforce linear range*. ::: {.callout-tip} ## In the app Use the arrow keys ↑ / ↓ to step through the rows of table 4.1 and ← / → to switch the mode; the figure follows at once. With the processing option *Log scale for calibration curve fitting*, the figure starts with log axes, which show the low concentrations better. :::
